claims.text: Superconducting properties such as Tc and Hc2 in high-entropy superconducting alloys are governed primarily by effective electron count rather than high-entropy disorder.
Increasing the effective electron count through compositional tuning should enhance superconductivity under high pressure.
High pressure stabilizes the overall crystal structure of the alloy.
The (TaNb)-(ZrHfTi) high-entropy alloy family exhibits superconductivity at ambient pressure despite substantial configurational disorder.
The alloy (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 has an ambient-pressure Tc of about 7.8 K and retains a zero-resistance superconducting state up to 190.6 GPa.
Samples with different compositions can be prepared with nearly identical configurational disorder while varying the electronic composition.
Prior high-pressure testing of the relevant alloy system has extended to approximately 190 GPa.
High-pressure treatment minimizes pressure-induced lattice distortions.
High-pressure treatment minimizes disorder-related electronic scattering.
Pressure-induced crystallographic stabilization decouples electron-count effects from disorder effects.
Atomic-scale disorder can impair superconductivity in high-entropy superconducting materials.
Superconductivity is more sensitive to the density of states at the Fermi level than to configurational disorder.
Compositional changes alter the alloy's effective electron count.
Changes in effective electron count modify Cooper pairing and thereby change Tc and Hc2.
At approximately constant disorder and high pressure, samples with higher effective electron counts will have higher Tc and possibly higher Hc2 than samples with lower electron counts.
Changes in Tc will correlate more strongly with effective electron count than with the degree of high-entropy mixing.
The proposed relationship is limited to pressure ranges without structural phase transitions and alloys without extreme local structural inhomogeneity.
Pressure-induced phase transitions or dominant extrinsic scattering mechanisms may invalidate the proposed electron-count relationship.
The relative quantitative contributions of electron count and disorder, and the ability of pressure to decouple them, remain uncertain and may be alloy-system dependent.
Failure of electron-count variation to produce systematic changes in Tc and Hc2 under structurally stable high pressure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The controlled comparison is described as comparing compositions under the same high-pressure conditions, but the named baseline is measured at ambient pressure. Pressure and composition would therefore differ simultaneously unless the baseline alloy is also measured at each test pressure.
